newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: U.S. signals tougher stance on Bosnia war crimes.
newsitem.headline: U.S. signals tougher stance on Bosnia war crimes.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Wednesday signalled a tougher stance on the tracking down of indicted war criminals in Bosnia.
Speaking at the U.N. war crimes Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia in the Hague, Albright said:
"Make no mistake, there is no statute of limitations on the crimes that were committed in Bosnia and Rwanda and no statute of limitations on American support for justice."
Albright was speaking after a 20-minute meeting with the tribunal's Chief Prosecutor, Louise Arbour.

Albright said she would press NATO allies to bring indictees to justice and also travel to Croatia, Serbia and Bosnia to insist that these three fully implement the Dayton peace accord, including complete cooperation with the war crimes tribunal in The Hague.
She said meeting the Dayton obligations was "a prerequisite" for these countries joining the international community and one these obligations was the transfer of indictees to the Hague.

The United States and its allies have come in for sharp criticism over the war-crimes issue as well from human-rights groups who note that the West has failed to back up tough rhetoric with concrete action -- for example, by having NATO peace troops in Bosnia grab notorious suspects who circulate freely in their midst.
Analysts say NATO has avoided arresting indictees for fear of retaliation against its peace troops by nationalist factions.

Albright continued: "I am going to deliver a tough message to Presidents Tudjman (of Croatia) and Milosevic (of Serbia) saying their lack of cooperation in this area is a roadblock to our increased cooperation with them.
"I am confident that a price will be paid for the atrocities that ravaged Bosnia for four years."
